```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 96)
options(width = 100, tibble.print_min = 5, tibble.print_max = 10, tibble.max_extra_cols = 6)
```

Before coverage is computed, the Countdown analysis asks four questions of the facility data: were the reports
sent, are there values that cannot be right, are values missing, and do related indicators agree. This guide goes
through the function for each, on the example dataset.

```{r}
library(cd2030.core)

cache <- load_cache_data(system.file("extdata", "kenya.xlsx", package = "cd2030.core"))
data <- cache$countdown_data
```

Three things are the same for every check:

- **The level.** `admin_level` is `"national"`, `"adminlevel_1"` (region) or `"district"`, and `region` keeps one
  region.
- **The result** is a table with a class of its own, which gives it a caption and usually a `plot()` method.
- **The threshold** is the reporting rate a district is expected to reach, in percent. 90 is used here.

## Reporting rates

The reporting rate is the share of expected monthly reports that were received, for each group of services.

```{r}
calculate_average_reporting_rate(data)
```

By region, as a chart:

```{r}
plot(calculate_average_reporting_rate(data, admin_level = "adminlevel_1"))
```

`calculate_district_reporting_rate()` counts districts: the percentage whose reporting rate reaches the threshold.

```{r}
calculate_district_reporting_rate(data, threshold = 90)
```

## Extreme outliers

A monthly value is an extreme outlier when it is more than five median absolute deviations from the district's
median for that indicator. The summary gives the percentage of values that are *not* outliers, so higher is
better.

```{r}
outliers <- calculate_outliers_summary(data, admin_level = "adminlevel_1")
plot(outliers, selection_type = "heat_map", indicator = "penta1")
```

`calculate_district_outlier_summary()` gives the percentage of districts with no extreme outlier in the year, and
`list_outlier_units()` returns the monthly values with their bounds, to find the months concerned.

```{r}
calculate_district_outlier_summary(data)[, c("year", "anc1_outlier5std", "penta1_outlier5std", "penta3_outlier5std")]
```

## Missing values

Completeness is the percentage of monthly values that are present.

```{r}
completeness <- calculate_completeness_summary(data, admin_level = "adminlevel_1")
plot(completeness, indicator = "penta1")
```

`calculate_district_completeness_summary()` gives the percentage of districts with no missing value, and
`list_missing_units()` names the districts and months where an indicator is missing.

```{r}
list_missing_units(data, indicator = "low_bweight")
```

## Consistency between indicators

Some indicators should move together: nearly every woman who attends a first antenatal visit has a child who
receives a first dose of pentavalent vaccine, and the first dose is a little more common than the third. The ratio
of each pair is compared with the ratio expected from survey coverage, the last row of the table.

```{r}
cache$ratios_summary
```

```{r}
plot(cache$ratios_summary)
```

## The overall score

`calculate_overall_score()` brings the checks together, one row per measure and one column per year. The last row
is the year's data quality score.

```{r}
score <- calculate_overall_score(data, threshold = 90)
score[, c("no", "Data Quality Metrics", "2021", "2022", "2023")]
```

## Changing how a chart looks

Every chart in the package takes the same arguments for its text: `title`, `subtitle`, `caption`, `x_title`,
`y_title` and `legend_title`. Anything else about its look is a chart option, given by name: the background, fonts,
sizes, the legend, the grid, the colours.

```{r}
rates <- calculate_average_reporting_rate(data, admin_level = "adminlevel_1")

plot(rates,
     title = "Reporting by region", subtitle = "All services", x_title = "Region", legend_title = "Rate",
     background_color = "grey96", font_family = "serif", legend_position = "right")
```

To give several charts one look, make the options once and pass them as `options`.

```{r}
look <- cd_chart_options(font_family = "serif", background_color = "grey96", text_scale = 0.9)

plot(calculate_district_reporting_rate(data, threshold = 90), title = "Districts reporting on time", options = look)
```

`?cd_plot_arguments` describes the shared arguments and `?cd_chart_options` lists every option.

## Through the dataset object

The `CacheConnection` holds each of these tables, computed once with the threshold it has stored and kept until
something they depend on changes. This is what the apps' pages read.

```{r}
cache$set_performance_threshold(90)
cache$reporting_rate_national
```

`?CacheConnection` lists them all (`reporting_rate_*`, `completeness_*`, `outliers_*`, `ratios_summary`,
`overall_score`).

## Acting on what you find

- **A year too poor to use** can be left out of the analysis: `cache$set_excluded_years(2019)`.
- **Under-reporting, outliers and missing values** are corrected by adjustment, the next step:
  `vignette("coverage")`.
- **A written summary**: `export_report(cache, report_presets("en")[["data_quality"]], "data-quality.docx")` writes
  the standard data quality report as a Word document.
